description: Marasmus is a severe form of acute malnutrition caused by prolonged inadequate intake of calories, protein, and other nutrients. It is most common in infants under 12 months and results in extreme wasting of muscle and fat. Without urgent treatment, it carries a high risk of death from infection, hypoglycemia, or organ failure.
symptoms: extreme weight loss (<60% expected weight for age)
prominent ribs, spine, and shoulder blades
visual_indicators: severely thin limbs with no fat cover
immediate_actions: Refer to inpatient therapeutic feeding center (TFC)
content:
Marasmus is a severe form of acute malnutrition caused by prolonged inadequate intake of calories, protein, and other nutrients. It is most common in infants under 12 months and results in extreme wasting of muscle and fat. Without urgent treatment, it carries a high risk of death from infection, hypoglycemia, or organ failure.
Symptoms: extreme weight loss (<60% expected weight for age), severe muscle wasting, prominent ribs, spine, and shoulder blades, sunken eyes and temples, loss of subcutaneous fat, irritability or lethargy
Visual signs: severely thin limbs with no fat cover, skin hanging loosely ('baggy pants' appearance), aged or 'old man' facial appearance, visible bones and joints

description: Kwashiorkor is severe protein malnutrition with relatively preserved caloric intake, leading to characteristic pitting edema and fatty liver enlargement. It occurs primarily in children aged 1–5 years after weaning and is associated with antioxidant deficiency and aflatoxin exposure. It carries a high mortality if untreated.
symptoms: bilateral pitting edema of feet and legs
weight may appear normal or high due to edema
visual_indicators: pale or reddish discolored hair (flag sign)
content:
Kwashiorkor is severe protein malnutrition with relatively preserved caloric intake, leading to characteristic pitting edema and fatty liver enlargement. It occurs primarily in children aged 1–5 years after weaning and is associated with antioxidant deficiency and aflatoxin exposure. It carries a high mortality if untreated.
Symptoms: bilateral pitting edema of feet and legs, enlarged abdomen (ascites), moon face (facial edema), fatigue and apathy, skin lesions and hair discoloration, weight may appear normal or high due to edema
Visual signs: swollen feet and legs, distended belly, pale or reddish discolored hair (flag sign), flaky paint dermatosis, sad/apathetic facial expression

description: Iron deficiency anemia occurs when insufficient iron reduces hemoglobin production, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. It is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide and disproportionately affects young children and pregnant women. Presentation ranges from asymptomatic to severe fatigue and impaired cognitive development.
immediate_actions: Start oral iron supplementation (3–6 mg/kg/day elemental iron)
content:
Iron deficiency anemia occurs when insufficient iron reduces hemoglobin production, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. It is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide and disproportionately affects young children and pregnant women. Presentation ranges from asymptomatic to severe fatigue and impaired cognitive development.
Symptoms: fatigue and weakness, pallor (pale skin, conjunctiva, palms), shortness of breath on exertion, poor appetite (pica — eating non-food items), poor concentration and developmental delay, frequent infections
Visual signs: pale inner eyelids (conjunctival pallor), pale lips and tongue, spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) in chronic cases

description: Rickets is a skeletal disorder in children caused by vitamin D or calcium deficiency, resulting in soft and weakened bones that may deform under normal body weight. It most commonly presents between 6 months and 2 years of age when bone growth is rapid. Early detection and supplementation are critical to prevent lasting deformity.
visual_indicators: enlarged skull or delayed fontanelle closure
immediate_actions: Start high-dose vitamin D supplementation per WHO/national protocol
Calcium supplementation if dietary intake is low
content:
Rickets is a skeletal disorder in children caused by vitamin D or calcium deficiency, resulting in soft and weakened bones that may deform under normal body weight. It most commonly presents between 6 months and 2 years of age when bone growth is rapid. Early detection and supplementation are critical to prevent lasting deformity.
Symptoms: bowed legs or knock knees, bone pain and tenderness, delayed tooth eruption, stunted growth, muscle weakness, large forehead (frontal bossing), chest deformities (rachitic rosary)
Visual signs: bowed legs or X-shaped legs, prominent wrist and ankle bones, enlarged skull or delayed fontanelle closure, pigeon chest deformity

description: Zinc deficiency results in impaired immune function, growth retardation, and skin changes, often appearing alongside other nutritional deficiencies. It is common in children consuming low-diversity diets in low-income countries. It is a key contributor to increased diarrhea and pneumonia severity.
visual_indicators: poor wound healing visible on skin
future_warnings: increased frequency and severity of diarrhea
immediate_actions: Oral zinc supplementation (10–20 mg/day per WHO)
Zinc included in diarrhea management protocol (10–14 days)
content:
Zinc deficiency results in impaired immune function, growth retardation, and skin changes, often appearing alongside other nutritional deficiencies. It is common in children consuming low-diversity diets in low-income countries. It is a key contributor to increased diarrhea and pneumonia severity.
Symptoms: growth retardation and short stature, diarrhea, poor appetite, delayed wound healing, hair loss, skin rashes and lesions, impaired taste and smell
Visual signs: perioral and periorbital skin lesions, alopecia (hair thinning), poor wound healing visible on skin

description: Iodine deficiency impairs thyroid hormone production, affecting brain development and metabolic regulation. In children, it causes goiter and cognitive impairment; in pregnant women, it can result in cretinism in the newborn. It remains a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability globally.
symptoms: intellectual disability (in severe or congenital cases)
future_warnings: irreversible intellectual disability if in utero
immediate_actions: Refer for thyroid evaluation if goiter present
content:
Iodine deficiency impairs thyroid hormone production, affecting brain development and metabolic regulation. In children, it causes goiter and cognitive impairment; in pregnant women, it can result in cretinism in the newborn. It remains a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability globally.
Symptoms: visible neck swelling (goiter), fatigue and sluggishness, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, intellectual disability (in severe or congenital cases)
Visual signs: visible goiter (enlarged thyroid in neck), puffy face, dull affect in severe cases

description: Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) is a leading cause of preventable blindness in children and increases mortality from common infections including measles and diarrhea. It begins with night blindness and can progress to corneal ulceration and permanent vision loss. Supplementation twice yearly is a standard public health intervention.
visual_indicators: white foamy spots on white of eye (Bitot's spots)
child bumping into objects in dim light
future_warnings: higher risk of maternal mortality during pregnancy
immediate_actions: Vitamin A supplementation (high-dose per WHO schedule)
Dietary counseling on vitamin A-rich foods
content:
Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) is a leading cause of preventable blindness in children and increases mortality from common infections including measles and diarrhea. It begins with night blindness and can progress to corneal ulceration and permanent vision loss. Supplementation twice yearly is a standard public health intervention.
Symptoms: night blindness (early sign), dry eyes (xerophthalmia), Bitot's spots on conjunctiva, corneal ulceration (severe), increased frequency of infections, poor skin integrity
Visual signs: white foamy spots on white of eye (Bitot's spots), dull, dry cornea, child bumping into objects in dim light

description: Measles is a highly contagious viral disease spread by respiratory droplets, causing high fever, rash, and cough. It is a major cause of death in malnourished and unvaccinated children, as it severely suppresses immunity for weeks. Complications include pneumonia, encephalitis, and blindness.
symptoms: blotchy red rash starting on face and spreading downward
Koplik's spots inside the mouth (early sign)
visual_indicators: maculopapular rash from head to toe
tiny white spots on inner cheeks (Koplik's spots)
future_warnings: corneal ulcer → blindness (in vitamin A-deficient children)
immune amnesia increasing infection risk for months
content:
Measles is a highly contagious viral disease spread by respiratory droplets, causing high fever, rash, and cough. It is a major cause of death in malnourished and unvaccinated children, as it severely suppresses immunity for weeks. Complications include pneumonia, encephalitis, and blindness.
Symptoms: high fever (>38.5°C), cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis (red eyes), blotchy red rash starting on face and spreading downward, Koplik's spots inside the mouth (early sign)
Visual signs: maculopapular rash from head to toe, red watery eyes, tiny white spots on inner cheeks (Koplik's spots)

description: Mumps is a viral infection primarily causing painful swelling of the salivary glands, especially the parotid glands. It spreads via respiratory droplets and saliva and is preventable by the MMR vaccine. Complications are rare but include orchitis, meningitis, and hearing loss.
future_warnings: orchitis in post-pubertal males (may affect fertility)
immediate_actions: Symptomatic treatment: pain relief, fluids, soft diet
Isolate child for 5 days after swelling onset
content:
Mumps is a viral infection primarily causing painful swelling of the salivary glands, especially the parotid glands. It spreads via respiratory droplets and saliva and is preventable by the MMR vaccine. Complications are rare but include orchitis, meningitis, and hearing loss.
Symptoms: fever, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, loss of appetite, painful swelling of cheeks/jaw (parotitis)
Visual signs: bilateral or unilateral puffy cheeks, swollen jaw area, tenderness on jaw palpation

description: Rubella (German measles) is a mild viral illness in children but poses severe danger during early pregnancy, causing congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) with heart defects, deafness, and blindness. The disease spreads via respiratory droplets and is preventable with MMR vaccine. Most children recover uneventfully within a week.
symptoms: pink-red rash starting on face, spreading to body (lasts ~3 days)
visual_indicators: fine pink rash on face spreading downward
future_warnings: congenital rubella syndrome in exposed fetuses (deafness, heart defects, blindness)
content:
Rubella (German measles) is a mild viral illness in children but poses severe danger during early pregnancy, causing congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) with heart defects, deafness, and blindness. The disease spreads via respiratory droplets and is preventable with MMR vaccine. Most children recover uneventfully within a week.
Symptoms: mild fever, pink-red rash starting on face, spreading to body (lasts ~3 days), swollen lymph nodes (post-auricular and occipital), joint pain (especially in adolescent girls), sore throat, red eyes
Visual signs: fine pink rash on face spreading downward, swollen lymph nodes behind ears, mild conjunctival redness

description: Pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterized by paroxysmal coughing fits followed by an inspiratory 'whoop.' It is most dangerous in infants under 6 months, who may stop breathing during coughing spells. The DTP vaccine provides effective prevention.
symptoms: cyanosis (blue color) during coughing in infants
visual_indicators: child turning red or blue during cough
distressed facial expression during coughing fit
future_warnings: apnea and respiratory failure in infants
immediate_actions: Isolate patient for 5 days after antibiotics started
Report to public health; trace contacts
content:
Pertussis (whooping cough) is a highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, characterized by paroxysmal coughing fits followed by an inspiratory 'whoop.' It is most dangerous in infants under 6 months, who may stop breathing during coughing spells. The DTP vaccine provides effective prevention.
Symptoms: prolonged coughing spells (paroxysms), inspiratory whoop after cough, post-cough vomiting, cyanosis (blue color) during coughing in infants, apnea in infants <6 months, runny nose in initial phase
Visual signs: child turning red or blue during cough, distressed facial expression during coughing fit, visible exhaustion after coughing spells

description: Diphtheria is a serious bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, producing a toxin that creates a tough gray membrane in the throat that can cause airway obstruction. The toxin also damages the heart and nervous system. It is preventable through DTP vaccination and is now rare in immunized populations.
symptoms: gray-white membrane covering tonsils and throat
content:
Diphtheria is a serious bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, producing a toxin that creates a tough gray membrane in the throat that can cause airway obstruction. The toxin also damages the heart and nervous system. It is preventable through DTP vaccination and is now rare in immunized populations.
Symptoms: sore throat and mild fever, gray-white membrane covering tonsils and throat, neck swelling ('bull neck'), hoarse voice and barking cough, difficulty swallowing, stridor (noisy breathing)
Visual signs: gray pseudomembrane visible on throat/tonsils, bull neck appearance (cervical lymphadenopathy), child appearing toxic and ill

description: Tetanus is a life-threatening infection caused by Clostridium tetani toxin, producing uncontrolled muscle spasms and rigidity. It enters through wounds, burns, or the umbilical stump in neonates (neonatal tetanus). It is preventable through vaccination and proper wound care, and requires intensive hospital management.
symptoms: muscle spasms triggered by stimuli (light, sound, touch)
visual_indicators: risus sardonicus (fixed smile due to facial muscle spasm)
future_warnings: respiratory failure from chest muscle spasm
age_group: All ages; neonates especially at risk
content:
Tetanus is a life-threatening infection caused by Clostridium tetani toxin, producing uncontrolled muscle spasms and rigidity. It enters through wounds, burns, or the umbilical stump in neonates (neonatal tetanus). It is preventable through vaccination and proper wound care, and requires intensive hospital management.
Symptoms: painful muscle stiffness (jaw — 'lockjaw', neck, abdomen), muscle spasms triggered by stimuli (light, sound, touch), difficulty swallowing, arching of the back (opisthotonus), fever, autonomic instability
Visual signs: trismus (clenched jaw that won't open), risus sardonicus (fixed smile due to facial muscle spasm), rigid, arched body posture

description: Poliomyelitis is a viral infection caused by poliovirus that can destroy motor neurons, leading to irreversible limb paralysis. Most infections are asymptomatic or cause mild flu-like illness; fewer than 1% develop paralysis. It is targeted for global eradication through oral and inactivated polio vaccines.
visual_indicators: sudden asymmetric limb weakness or paralysis
limb may appear limp and smaller than other
child unable to walk who was walking before
immediate_actions: Report to public health immediately (notifiable disease)
content:
Poliomyelitis is a viral infection caused by poliovirus that can destroy motor neurons, leading to irreversible limb paralysis. Most infections are asymptomatic or cause mild flu-like illness; fewer than 1% develop paralysis. It is targeted for global eradication through oral and inactivated polio vaccines.
Symptoms: fever, fatigue, headache (early), stiff neck and back, muscle pain and weakness, asymmetric flaccid paralysis (in paralytic cases), difficulty breathing (if respiratory muscles affected)
Visual signs: sudden asymmetric limb weakness or paralysis, limb may appear limp and smaller than other, child unable to walk who was walking before

description: Malaria is a life-threatening parasitic infection transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, most commonly caused by Plasmodium falciparum in sub-Saharan Africa. It causes cyclical fever, chills, and anemia, and can rapidly progress to severe disease including cerebral malaria in young children. Early diagnosis and artemisinin-based treatment are essential.
immediate_actions: Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or blood smear immediately
content:
Malaria is a life-threatening parasitic infection transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, most commonly caused by Plasmodium falciparum in sub-Saharan Africa. It causes cyclical fever, chills, and anemia, and can rapidly progress to severe disease including cerebral malaria in young children. Early diagnosis and artemisinin-based treatment are essential.
Symptoms: cyclical fever and chills, headache, vomiting, fatigue and pallor, spleen enlargement, anemia, rapid breathing
Visual signs: pallor of conjunctiva and palms, jaundice in severe cases, splenomegaly (palpable enlarged spleen), rapid deterioration in young child

description: Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral illness caused by the dengue virus (DENV 1–4), presenting with sudden high fever, severe headache, and body pain. Severe dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome) can develop rapidly and is life-threatening. No specific antiviral exists; management is supportive with careful fluid management.
future_warnings: death in severe dengue without fluid management
immediate_actions: Monitor hematocrit and platelet count daily
Adequate oral fluids or IV fluids if severe
Avoid NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen — increase bleeding risk)
Hospitalize if warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding
content:
Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral illness caused by the dengue virus (DENV 1–4), presenting with sudden high fever, severe headache, and body pain. Severe dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome) can develop rapidly and is life-threatening. No specific antiviral exists; management is supportive with careful fluid management.
Symptoms: sudden high fever (39–40°C), severe headache, pain behind eyes, joint and muscle pain ('breakbone fever'), rash (appears 3–4 days after fever), nausea and vomiting, bleeding gums or nosebleeds
Visual signs: flushed face with fever, maculopapular or petechial rash, positive tourniquet test (petechiae on forearm), spontaneous bleeding in severe cases

description: Typhoid fever is a systemic bacterial infection caused by Salmonella typhi, transmitted through contaminated food and water. It presents with sustained high fever, abdominal pain, and characteristic rose spots on the abdomen. Without antibiotic treatment, serious complications such as intestinal perforation can occur.
symptoms: sustained high fever (stepwise rise over days)
visual_indicators: rose spots (faint pink spots) on chest/abdomen
relative bradycardia (slow heart rate despite fever)
immediate_actions: Start antibiotics (azithromycin or ceftriaxone for children)
Hospitalize if severe or complications suspected
content:
Typhoid fever is a systemic bacterial infection caused by Salmonella typhi, transmitted through contaminated food and water. It presents with sustained high fever, abdominal pain, and characteristic rose spots on the abdomen. Without antibiotic treatment, serious complications such as intestinal perforation can occur.
Symptoms: sustained high fever (stepwise rise over days), headache and fatigue, abdominal pain and tenderness, rose-colored spots on abdomen, constipation or diarrhea, cough, enlarged spleen and liver
Visual signs: rose spots (faint pink spots) on chest/abdomen, relative bradycardia (slow heart rate despite fever), ill-appearing child with high fever

description: Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, most commonly affecting the lungs but capable of spreading to lymph nodes, bones, meninges, and other organs. Children under 5 and HIV-positive children are at highest risk of severe or disseminated disease. Long-term multi-drug treatment is required.
symptoms: weight loss or failure to thrive
visual_indicators: enlarged non-tender lymph nodes in neck
immediate_actions: Sputum or gastric aspirate for culture/GeneXpert
content:
Pediatric tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, most commonly affecting the lungs but capable of spreading to lymph nodes, bones, meninges, and other organs. Children under 5 and HIV-positive children are at highest risk of severe or disseminated disease. Long-term multi-drug treatment is required.
Symptoms: persistent cough >2 weeks, weight loss or failure to thrive, prolonged fever (>2 weeks), night sweats, fatigue, lymph node enlargement (cervical or hilar), loss of appetite
Visual signs: visible weight loss and wasting, enlarged non-tender lymph nodes in neck, child appearing chronically ill

description: Septicemia (sepsis) is a life-threatening systemic response to infection in which the body's immune response begins to damage its own tissues and organs. In neonates and young children it presents subtly with temperature instability, poor feeding, and lethargy. Rapid recognition and broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy are critical to survival.
symptoms: high or low temperature (fever or hypothermia)
visual_indicators: child unresponsive or difficult to rouse
immediate_actions: Urgent IV access and blood culture before antibiotics
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately (do not delay)
content:
Septicemia (sepsis) is a life-threatening systemic response to infection in which the body's immune response begins to damage its own tissues and organs. In neonates and young children it presents subtly with temperature instability, poor feeding, and lethargy. Rapid recognition and broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy are critical to survival.
Symptoms: high or low temperature (fever or hypothermia), rapid heart rate (tachycardia), rapid breathing, poor feeding or lethargy, bulging fontanelle in infants, rash (petechiae in meningococcal sepsis), reduced urine output
Visual signs: mottled or grayish skin, capillary refill >3 seconds, sunken or bulging fontanelle, child unresponsive or difficult to rouse

description: Roseola (exanthem subitum) is a common viral infection in infants caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), presenting with 3–5 days of high fever that resolves abruptly, followed by a pink rash on the trunk. It is generally benign and self-limiting, though febrile seizures may occur during the high fever phase.
symptoms: 3–5 days of high fever (39–40°C) without obvious cause
rose-pink rash appears after fever breaks (starts on trunk, spreads to neck and arms)
visual_indicators: pink macular/maculopapular rash on trunk after fever resolves
immediate_actions: Reassure parents — rash after fever is a good sign (fever breaking)
content:
Roseola (exanthem subitum) is a common viral infection in infants caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), presenting with 3–5 days of high fever that resolves abruptly, followed by a pink rash on the trunk. It is generally benign and self-limiting, though febrile seizures may occur during the high fever phase.
Symptoms: 3–5 days of high fever (39–40°C) without obvious cause, fever breaks suddenly, rose-pink rash appears after fever breaks (starts on trunk, spreads to neck and arms), mild irritability, swollen neck lymph nodes
Visual signs: pink macular/maculopapular rash on trunk after fever resolves, well-appearing child despite high fever

description: Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum) is a mild viral illness caused by Parvovirus B19, producing a distinctive 'slapped cheek' rash in children. It is generally benign in healthy children but can cause severe anemia in those with sickle cell disease, or hydrops fetalis if contracted during pregnancy.
symptoms: bright red rash on cheeks ('slapped cheek' appearance)
lacy reticular rash on arms and legs
visual_indicators: lacy pink-red rash on limbs and trunk
future_warnings: aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease patients
fetal hydrops if mother infected during pregnancy (spontaneous abortion risk)
immediate_actions: Isolate from pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals
Monitor hemoglobin in children with hemolytic anemias
No specific antiviral needed for healthy children
content:
Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum) is a mild viral illness caused by Parvovirus B19, producing a distinctive 'slapped cheek' rash in children. It is generally benign in healthy children but can cause severe anemia in those with sickle cell disease, or hydrops fetalis if contracted during pregnancy.
Symptoms: bright red rash on cheeks ('slapped cheek' appearance), lacy reticular rash on arms and legs, mild fever before rash appears, joint pain (more common in adults), mild cold symptoms preceding rash
Visual signs: bright red flushed cheeks (bilateral), lacy pink-red rash on limbs and trunk

description: Scarlet fever is a bacterial illness caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS) toxin, producing a sandpaper-like red rash, high fever, and 'strawberry tongue.' It primarily affects school-age children and requires antibiotic treatment to prevent serious complications including rheumatic heart disease.
symptoms: sandpaper-texture red rash (starts on neck/chest, spares face)
flushed face with pale area around mouth
visual_indicators: Pastia's lines (rash darkening in skin folds)
future_warnings: rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease (if untreated)
immediate_actions: Isolate for 24 hours after antibiotics started
Screen household contacts if recurrent cases
content:
Scarlet fever is a bacterial illness caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS) toxin, producing a sandpaper-like red rash, high fever, and 'strawberry tongue.' It primarily affects school-age children and requires antibiotic treatment to prevent serious complications including rheumatic heart disease.
Symptoms: sudden high fever, sore throat, headache, sandpaper-texture red rash (starts on neck/chest, spares face), flushed face with pale area around mouth, strawberry tongue (red, bumpy tongue), nausea
Visual signs: red sandpaper rash on trunk, circumoral pallor (pale ring around mouth), bright red strawberry tongue, Pastia's lines (rash darkening in skin folds)

description: Pneumonia is an acute lung infection causing inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli, significantly impairing oxygenation. It is the leading single infectious cause of death in children under 5 globally. Bacterial pneumonia (often Streptococcus pneumoniae) requires antibiotic treatment while viral forms are managed supportively.
immediate_actions: WHO IMCI: count breaths per minute to classify severity
Hospitalize if danger signs (chest in-drawing, cyanosis, unable to feed)
content:
Pneumonia is an acute lung infection causing inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli, significantly impairing oxygenation. It is the leading single infectious cause of death in children under 5 globally. Bacterial pneumonia (often Streptococcus pneumoniae) requires antibiotic treatment while viral forms are managed supportively.
Symptoms: fast breathing (tachypnea), chest in-drawing, cough, fever, nasal flaring, cyanosis (blue lips/fingernails), grunting, poor feeding in infants
Visual signs: chest in-drawing (subcostal or intercostal recession), nasal flaring, visible labored breathing, cyanosis in severe cases

description: Bronchiolitis is a common lower respiratory tract infection in infants caused primarily by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), causing inflammation and mucus buildup in the small airways. It presents with wheeze, cough, and respiratory distress, and is the leading cause of hospitalization in infants under 12 months. Management is supportive.
visual_indicators: child struggling to feed due to breathlessness
future_warnings: apnea in very young infants (<3 months)
increased risk of recurrent wheeze/asthma later in life
immediate_actions: Supportive: small frequent feeds, nasal suctioning
Hospitalize if <3 months, unable to feed, SpO2 low, or worsening
No role for antibiotics, steroids, or bronchodilators routinely
content:
Bronchiolitis is a common lower respiratory tract infection in infants caused primarily by Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), causing inflammation and mucus buildup in the small airways. It presents with wheeze, cough, and respiratory distress, and is the leading cause of hospitalization in infants under 12 months. Management is supportive.
Symptoms: runny nose progressing to cough, wheeze (high-pitched whistling sound), rapid breathing, difficulty feeding, low-grade fever, subcostal in-drawing, irritability
Visual signs: visible wheeze and chest retractions, nasal flaring, child struggling to feed due to breathlessness

description: Croup is a viral upper airway infection (most commonly parainfluenza) causing subglottic edema that produces the characteristic barking cough and inspiratory stridor. It typically affects children aged 6 months to 3 years and is usually mild, though severe stridor at rest requires urgent corticosteroid and possibly nebulized adrenaline treatment.
symptoms: mild runny nose before cough onset
visual_indicators: child with barking cough audible across the room
future_warnings: need for intubation in severe cases
immediate_actions: Oral dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg single dose) — cornerstone of treatment
Hospitalize if stridor at rest, cyanosis, or no improvement
content:
Croup is a viral upper airway infection (most commonly parainfluenza) causing subglottic edema that produces the characteristic barking cough and inspiratory stridor. It typically affects children aged 6 months to 3 years and is usually mild, though severe stridor at rest requires urgent corticosteroid and possibly nebulized adrenaline treatment.
Symptoms: barking cough (seal-like), inspiratory stridor, hoarse voice, low-grade fever, mild runny nose before cough onset, worsening at night
Visual signs: child with barking cough audible across the room, stridor at rest (severe sign), neck retractions in severe croup, anxious posture (sitting forward)

description: Pediatric asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by recurrent episodes of wheezing, cough, and shortness of breath caused by bronchospasm and airway hyper-responsiveness. Triggers include viral infections, allergens, exercise, and smoke. Long-term inhaled corticosteroids are the mainstay of persistent asthma control.
symptoms: symptoms triggered by exercise, cold air, or infections
immediate_actions: Salbutamol (albuterol) inhaler — first-line for acute attack
Hospitalize if poor response, cyanosis, or altered consciousness
content:
Pediatric asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by recurrent episodes of wheezing, cough, and shortness of breath caused by bronchospasm and airway hyper-responsiveness. Triggers include viral infections, allergens, exercise, and smoke. Long-term inhaled corticosteroids are the mainstay of persistent asthma control.
Symptoms: recurrent wheeze, persistent or nighttime cough, shortness of breath with activity, chest tightness, symptoms triggered by exercise, cold air, or infections, improvement with bronchodilators
Visual signs: audible wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, accessory muscle use during exacerbation, hunched posture trying to breathe

description: Acute upper respiratory infections (ARIs) encompass common cold, rhinitis, pharyngitis, and sinusitis, predominantly caused by viruses (rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus). They are the most frequent illnesses in childhood and generally self-limiting. Antibiotics are not indicated for viral ARIs.
future_warnings: secondary bacterial sinusitis or otitis media
pneumonia in malnourished or immunocompromised children
immediate_actions: Supportive care: fluids, rest, saline nasal drops
Avoid antibiotics unless bacterial superinfection confirmed
content:
Acute upper respiratory infections (ARIs) encompass common cold, rhinitis, pharyngitis, and sinusitis, predominantly caused by viruses (rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus). They are the most frequent illnesses in childhood and generally self-limiting. Antibiotics are not indicated for viral ARIs.
Symptoms: runny or blocked nose, sneezing, sore throat, mild fever, cough, headache, general malaise
Visual signs: nasal discharge (clear to yellow-green), red throat on exam, watery eyes

description: Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is inflammation of the stomach and intestines causing diarrhea and vomiting, most commonly caused by rotavirus in young children. It is a leading cause of child mortality due to dehydration. Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is the cornerstone of treatment; rotavirus vaccine has dramatically reduced severe cases.
visual_indicators: poor skin turgor (skin pinch returns slowly)
immediate_actions: IV Ringer's lactate if severe dehydration or vomiting prevents oral rehydration
content:
Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is inflammation of the stomach and intestines causing diarrhea and vomiting, most commonly caused by rotavirus in young children. It is a leading cause of child mortality due to dehydration. Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is the cornerstone of treatment; rotavirus vaccine has dramatically reduced severe cases.
Symptoms: watery diarrhea (>3 stools/day), vomiting, fever, abdominal cramps, decreased urine output (dehydration sign), sunken eyes (dehydration sign), dry mouth and no tears
Visual signs: sunken eyes, dry mouth and tongue, poor skin turgor (skin pinch returns slowly), lethargic child

description: Cholera is an acute diarrheal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae, producing profuse watery 'rice-water' stool and vomiting that can cause life-threatening dehydration within hours. It spreads through contaminated water and food and is a major threat during disasters and outbreaks. Rapid rehydration is life-saving.
symptoms: sudden onset profuse watery diarrhea ('rice-water' stool)
visual_indicators: signs of severe dehydration in hours
immediate_actions: IV Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration (100 ml/kg over 3 hours for children)
content:
Cholera is an acute diarrheal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae, producing profuse watery 'rice-water' stool and vomiting that can cause life-threatening dehydration within hours. It spreads through contaminated water and food and is a major threat during disasters and outbreaks. Rapid rehydration is life-saving.
Symptoms: sudden onset profuse watery diarrhea ('rice-water' stool), vomiting, muscle cramps (from electrolyte loss), rapid dehydration, no fever typically, sunken eyes and cheeks, cold clammy skin
Visual signs: large volumes of watery stool, rapidly sunken eyes and skin, signs of severe dehydration in hours, rice-water appearance of stool

description: Helminthiasis refers to intestinal worm infections (roundworm, hookworm, whipworm, tapeworm) transmitted through contaminated soil or food, extremely common in tropical and low-income settings. Chronic infection causes malnutrition, anemia, and growth retardation in children. Mass drug administration (deworming) is a key public health strategy.
visual_indicators: visible worms or segments in stool
future_warnings: intestinal obstruction from heavy roundworm burden
immediate_actions: Albendazole (400 mg single dose) or mebendazole (500 mg single dose)
Part of biannual deworming program for school children
Hygiene education: hand washing, safe food/water
content:
Helminthiasis refers to intestinal worm infections (roundworm, hookworm, whipworm, tapeworm) transmitted through contaminated soil or food, extremely common in tropical and low-income settings. Chronic infection causes malnutrition, anemia, and growth retardation in children. Mass drug administration (deworming) is a key public health strategy.
Symptoms: abdominal pain and bloating, diarrhea or loose stools, visible worms in stool (roundworm), nutritional deficiencies and anemia, poor growth and weight gain, fatigue, itching around the anus (pinworm)
Visual signs: visible worms or segments in stool, abdominal distension, pallor from anemia

description: Giardiasis is a parasitic gut infection caused by Giardia lamblia, transmitted via contaminated water or person-to-person contact. It causes chronic watery or greasy diarrhea and malabsorption, contributing to growth failure in young children. Treatment with metronidazole is highly effective.
symptoms: chronic watery or greasy, foul-smelling diarrhea
future_warnings: lactose intolerance secondary to mucosal damage
failure to thrive in young children
immediate_actions: Stool microscopy or antigen test to confirm
content:
Giardiasis is a parasitic gut infection caused by Giardia lamblia, transmitted via contaminated water or person-to-person contact. It causes chronic watery or greasy diarrhea and malabsorption, contributing to growth failure in young children. Treatment with metronidazole is highly effective.
Symptoms: chronic watery or greasy, foul-smelling diarrhea, abdominal bloating and cramps, flatulence, nausea, fatigue, weight loss, malabsorption of fats and vitamins
Visual signs: frothy greasy stools, abdominal distension, weight loss visible over weeks

description: Amoebiasis is an intestinal infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, spread through contaminated food and water. It ranges from asymptomatic carriage to invasive dysentery with bloody diarrhea, and can spread to cause amoebic liver abscess. Treatment with metronidazole targets invasive disease.
visual_indicators: jaundice or fever suggesting liver abscess
immediate_actions: Stool microscopy or PCR for diagnosis
Metronidazole (35–50 mg/kg/day in 3 doses for 7–10 days)
Followed by diloxanide furoate to clear luminal infection
content:
Amoebiasis is an intestinal infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, spread through contaminated food and water. It ranges from asymptomatic carriage to invasive dysentery with bloody diarrhea, and can spread to cause amoebic liver abscess. Treatment with metronidazole targets invasive disease.
Symptoms: crampy abdominal pain, bloody or mucoid diarrhea (dysentery), tenesmus (urgent painful need to defecate), fever (in invasive disease), weight loss, right upper quadrant pain (liver abscess)
Visual signs: blood and mucus in stool, tender abdomen on palpation, jaundice or fever suggesting liver abscess

description: Chickenpox (varicella) is a highly contagious viral illness caused by Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), producing a pruritic vesicular rash in successive crops across the body. Most cases in healthy children are mild and self-limiting, but complications including bacterial superinfection, pneumonia, and encephalitis can occur, particularly in immunocompromised children.
symptoms: intensely itchy vesicular rash in multiple stages (macule→papule→vesicle→crust)
rash appears in crops over 3–5 days
rash on face, scalp, trunk, and limbs
visual_indicators: rash on scalp (unusual in other rashes)
future_warnings: bacterial superinfection of skin (streptococcal — necrotizing fasciitis risk)
immediate_actions: Isolate until all lesions crusted (~7 days)
Oral acyclovir for immunocompromised or severe disease
content:
Chickenpox (varicella) is a highly contagious viral illness caused by Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), producing a pruritic vesicular rash in successive crops across the body. Most cases in healthy children are mild and self-limiting, but complications including bacterial superinfection, pneumonia, and encephalitis can occur, particularly in immunocompromised children.
Symptoms: fever before rash, intensely itchy vesicular rash in multiple stages (macule→papule→vesicle→crust), rash appears in crops over 3–5 days, rash on face, scalp, trunk, and limbs, malaise and loss of appetite, headache
Visual signs: vesicles at multiple stages simultaneously (characteristic), rash on scalp (unusual in other rashes), crusting lesions alongside fresh vesicles

description: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) is a common contagious viral illness in young children caused by enteroviruses (Coxsackievirus A16, Enterovirus 71), producing painful oral ulcers and a distinctive rash on the palms, soles, and buttocks. Most cases are mild and self-limiting; however, EV71 strains can cause severe neurological complications.
symptoms: painful sores/ulcers in mouth (makes eating painful)
flat or raised red spots/blisters on palms of hands
visual_indicators: oral ulcers on tongue and inner cheeks
child refusing to eat due to mouth pain
future_warnings: pulmonary edema in severe EV71 cases
immediate_actions: Symptomatic care: pain relief, cool fluids, soft food
Isolate child from school/daycare until lesions resolve
Watch for neurological signs: tremors, drowsiness, rapid breathing
content:
Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) is a common contagious viral illness in young children caused by enteroviruses (Coxsackievirus A16, Enterovirus 71), producing painful oral ulcers and a distinctive rash on the palms, soles, and buttocks. Most cases are mild and self-limiting; however, EV71 strains can cause severe neurological complications.
Symptoms: fever (1–2 days before rash), painful sores/ulcers in mouth (makes eating painful), flat or raised red spots/blisters on palms of hands, spots on soles of feet, spots on buttocks and groin, irritability and poor feeding
Visual signs: blisters on palms and soles (pathognomonic), oral ulcers on tongue and inner cheeks, child refusing to eat due to mouth pain

description: Scabies is a highly contagious skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, producing intense nocturnal pruritus from the mite's burrowing under the skin. In malnourished children it can progress to crusted (Norwegian) scabies with thousands of mites, high infectivity, and severe secondary infections. Topical permethrin is first-line treatment.
symptoms: burrow tracks (thin wavy lines) between fingers, wrists, genitals
rash spreading to all family members
visual_indicators: linear burrows between fingers and toes
rash in finger webs, wrists, axilla, genitals
thick crusted plaques in crusted scabies
future_warnings: crusted scabies (highly contagious, very difficult to treat)
secondary bacterial infection → cellulitis or sepsis
post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis from infected scabies lesions
immediate_actions: 5% permethrin cream — apply head to toe, leave 8–12 hrs, repeat in 1 week
Wash all clothing and bedding in hot water
Oral ivermectin for crusted scabies (weight-based dosing)
content:
Scabies is a highly contagious skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, producing intense nocturnal pruritus from the mite's burrowing under the skin. In malnourished children it can progress to crusted (Norwegian) scabies with thousands of mites, high infectivity, and severe secondary infections. Topical permethrin is first-line treatment.
Symptoms: intense itching worse at night, burrow tracks (thin wavy lines) between fingers, wrists, genitals, papular or vesicular rash, secondary bacterial infection (impetigo), rash spreading to all family members
Visual signs: linear burrows between fingers and toes, rash in finger webs, wrists, axilla, genitals, excoriation marks from scratching, thick crusted plaques in crusted scabies

description: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp and hair shafts caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum), common in school-age children. It produces scaling, hair loss, and sometimes a painful kerion (inflammatory mass). Oral antifungals are required as topical treatment alone is insufficient.
symptoms: kerion (boggy, pus-filled mass) in inflammatory type
visual_indicators: circular scaly bald patches on scalp
broken stubby hairs at scalp level
kerion if inflammatory — looks like abscess
future_warnings: spread to other children in school/household
immediate_actions: Oral griseofulvin (20–25 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks) or oral terbinafine
Antifungal shampoo (selenium sulfide or ketoconazole) to reduce shedding
content:
Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp and hair shafts caused by dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum), common in school-age children. It produces scaling, hair loss, and sometimes a painful kerion (inflammatory mass). Oral antifungals are required as topical treatment alone is insufficient.
Symptoms: scaly patches on scalp, hair loss (alopecia) in affected areas, itching, broken hair stubs, cervical lymphadenopathy, kerion (boggy, pus-filled mass) in inflammatory type
Visual signs: circular scaly bald patches on scalp, broken stubby hairs at scalp level, kerion if inflammatory — looks like abscess, scaling with hair loss

description: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, presenting as honey-colored crusted lesions or fluid-filled blisters (bullous impetigo). It is highly contagious through direct contact and common in young children, particularly in warm humid climates or poor hygiene settings.
symptoms: honey-colored crusted sores on face (around nose and mouth) or limbs
weeping sores that spread by scratching
immediate_actions: Oral antibiotics (cefalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate) for extensive disease
Keep child home until 48 hours after starting antibiotics
content:
Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, presenting as honey-colored crusted lesions or fluid-filled blisters (bullous impetigo). It is highly contagious through direct contact and common in young children, particularly in warm humid climates or poor hygiene settings.
Symptoms: honey-colored crusted sores on face (around nose and mouth) or limbs, fluid-filled blisters (bullous impetigo — on trunk), itching, weeping sores that spread by scratching, mild local lymph node swelling
Visual signs: golden-yellow crusted lesions around nose/mouth, ruptured blisters with honey-colored crust, lesions spreading on exposed skin

description: Acute otitis media (AOM) is a bacterial or viral middle ear infection, the most common cause of childhood ear pain and a leading reason for antibiotic prescribing in children. It typically follows an upper respiratory infection. Most cases resolve spontaneously, but recurrent or untreated infections can cause hearing loss.
symptoms: ear pain (tugging at ear in infants)
ear discharge if tympanic membrane perforates
visual_indicators: red, bulging tympanic membrane on otoscopy
child pulling at one ear repeatedly
future_warnings: conductive hearing loss from recurrent infection
mastoiditis (spreading infection to bone behind ear)
immediate_actions: Watchful waiting for 48–72 hours in mild cases (>2 years)
Refer if recurrent (>3 episodes/year) for consideration of grommets
content:
Acute otitis media (AOM) is a bacterial or viral middle ear infection, the most common cause of childhood ear pain and a leading reason for antibiotic prescribing in children. It typically follows an upper respiratory infection. Most cases resolve spontaneously, but recurrent or untreated infections can cause hearing loss.
Symptoms: ear pain (tugging at ear in infants), fever, fussiness and irritability, difficulty sleeping, decreased hearing, ear discharge if tympanic membrane perforates, vomiting
Visual signs: red, bulging tympanic membrane on otoscopy, ear discharge (if perforated), child pulling at one ear repeatedly

description: Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils, commonly caused by viruses or Group A Streptococcus bacteria, presenting with severe sore throat, fever, and tonsillar enlargement. Streptococcal tonsillitis requires antibiotic treatment to prevent rheumatic fever. Recurrent tonsillitis may require tonsillectomy.
symptoms: swollen red tonsils (may have white exudate)
visual_indicators: swollen red tonsils with white patches/exudate
uvula may be displaced (peritonsillar abscess sign)
future_warnings: rheumatic fever from untreated streptococcal tonsillitis
obstructive sleep apnea from chronic enlargement
immediate_actions: Throat swab for rapid strep test
Penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days if strep confirmed/suspected
Hospitalize if drooling, trismus, or suspected abscess
content:
Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils, commonly caused by viruses or Group A Streptococcus bacteria, presenting with severe sore throat, fever, and tonsillar enlargement. Streptococcal tonsillitis requires antibiotic treatment to prevent rheumatic fever. Recurrent tonsillitis may require tonsillectomy.
Symptoms: severe sore throat, fever, difficulty swallowing, swollen red tonsils (may have white exudate), swollen tender cervical lymph nodes, headache, abdominal pain (children)
Visual signs: swollen red tonsils with white patches/exudate, uvula may be displaced (peritonsillar abscess sign), tender lymph nodes under jaw

description: Conjunctivitis (pink eye) is inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by viruses, bacteria, or allergens, producing red eyes with discharge. Bacterial conjunctivitis is treated with antibiotic eye drops; viral and allergic forms are managed symptomatically. Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) requires urgent treatment to prevent vision loss.
symptoms: discharge (watery in viral/allergic; purulent in bacterial)
future_warnings: corneal ulcer if untreated (especially in neonates with gonococcal conjunctivitis)
spreading to other eye or other children
immediate_actions: Antibiotic eye drops (chloramphenicol or fusidic acid) for bacterial type
Neonatal: ceftriaxone IV + saline irrigation for gonococcal
Hygiene: no sharing towels, frequent hand washing
content:
Conjunctivitis (pink eye) is inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by viruses, bacteria, or allergens, producing red eyes with discharge. Bacterial conjunctivitis is treated with antibiotic eye drops; viral and allergic forms are managed symptomatically. Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) requires urgent treatment to prevent vision loss.
Symptoms: red, pink eyes (one or both), discharge (watery in viral/allergic; purulent in bacterial), eyelids stuck together on waking, itching (allergic type), gritty sensation, mild photophobia
Visual signs: pink-red conjunctiva (white of eye), yellow-green pus discharge (bacterial), watery discharge (viral/allergic), eyelid swelling

description: Febrile seizures are convulsions triggered by fever in young children, typically occurring between 6 months and 5 years of age. Most are brief, generalized, and benign — they do not cause brain damage and do not indicate epilepsy. Parental education and reassurance are key, though fever management does not prevent recurrence.
symptoms: stiffening of body then rhythmic jerking
seizure >15 min or focal = complex (needs investigation)
visual_indicators: child unresponsive but breathing during seizure
future_warnings: 30% risk of recurrence (highest in first year)
complex febrile seizures may indicate underlying meningitis or encephalitis
epilepsy (slightly higher lifetime risk, but still low at ~2–5%)
immediate_actions: Do not put anything in mouth
Diazepam if seizure >5 min (rectal or IV)
Check for meningitis (lumbar puncture if <12 months or signs of meningism)
content:
Febrile seizures are convulsions triggered by fever in young children, typically occurring between 6 months and 5 years of age. Most are brief, generalized, and benign — they do not cause brain damage and do not indicate epilepsy. Parental education and reassurance are key, though fever management does not prevent recurrence.
Symptoms: generalized tonic-clonic seizure during fever, loss of consciousness, stiffening of body then rhythmic jerking, brief postictal drowsiness after seizure, seizure typically lasts <5 minutes (simple), seizure >15 min or focal = complex (needs investigation)
Visual signs: child convulsing with high fever, rhythmic jerking of limbs, child unresponsive but breathing during seizure, drowsy and confused immediately after

description: Meningitis is life-threatening inflammation of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord, caused by bacteria (Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae) or viruses. Bacterial meningitis in children requires emergency antibiotic treatment within 1 hour of clinical diagnosis. Presentation can be rapid and atypical in infants.
visual_indicators: child unable to touch chin to chest (neck stiffness)
non-blanching rash (glass test — rash visible through glass)
Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs on examination
immediate_actions: IV antibiotics immediately (do not wait for lumbar puncture if delay expected) — ceftriaxone
Notify public health; prophylax close contacts
content:
Meningitis is life-threatening inflammation of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord, caused by bacteria (Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae) or viruses. Bacterial meningitis in children requires emergency antibiotic treatment within 1 hour of clinical diagnosis. Presentation can be rapid and atypical in infants.
Symptoms: severe headache, stiff neck (nuchal rigidity), high fever, photophobia and phonophobia, vomiting, altered consciousness, bulging fontanelle (infants), non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (meningococcal)
Visual signs: child unable to touch chin to chest (neck stiffness), non-blanching rash (glass test — rash visible through glass), bulging fontanelle in infant, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs on examination

description: Kawasaki disease is an acute self-limiting vasculitis of unknown etiology affecting medium-sized arteries, most commonly in children under 5. It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in high-income countries due to coronary artery aneurysms. Prompt diagnosis and IVIG treatment within 10 days of fever onset dramatically reduce cardiac complications.
symptoms: red cracked lips and strawberry tongue
swollen red hands and feet (peeling in recovery phase)
visual_indicators: red palms and soles with subsequent peeling
future_warnings: coronary artery aneurysms (in up to 25% if untreated)
immediate_actions: IVIG (2 g/kg single infusion) within 10 days of fever
Echocardiogram at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6–8 weeks
Long-term cardiology follow-up for coronary involvement
content:
Kawasaki disease is an acute self-limiting vasculitis of unknown etiology affecting medium-sized arteries, most commonly in children under 5. It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in high-income countries due to coronary artery aneurysms. Prompt diagnosis and IVIG treatment within 10 days of fever onset dramatically reduce cardiac complications.
Symptoms: fever >5 days (required criterion), bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, red cracked lips and strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash on body, swollen red hands and feet (peeling in recovery phase), unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy (>1.5 cm)
Visual signs: bright red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, red palms and soles with subsequent peeling, red eyes without discharge, rash on trunk

description: Nephrotic syndrome in children is characterized by massive protein leakage into urine causing low blood proteins, generalized edema, and high cholesterol. The most common form (minimal change disease) responds well to corticosteroids. It is associated with increased infection risk, particularly from encapsulated bacteria.
symptoms: puffiness around eyes (periorbital edema — earliest sign)
visual_indicators: puffiness around eyes especially in mornings
future_warnings: steroid side effects with long-term treatment
immediate_actions: Urine dipstick (3+ or 4+ protein confirms nephrotic-range proteinuria)
content:
Nephrotic syndrome in children is characterized by massive protein leakage into urine causing low blood proteins, generalized edema, and high cholesterol. The most common form (minimal change disease) responds well to corticosteroids. It is associated with increased infection risk, particularly from encapsulated bacteria.
Symptoms: puffiness around eyes (periorbital edema — earliest sign), swelling of legs and abdomen, frothy urine, weight gain from fluid retention, reduced urine output, fatigue, loss of appetite
Visual signs: puffiness around eyes especially in mornings, swollen legs and abdomen, frothy or foamy urine

description: Intussusception is a surgical emergency where one segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent segment, causing bowel obstruction and ischemia. It is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children 3 months to 3 years. The classic triad is intermittent severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and red 'currant jelly' stool.
symptoms: sudden severe intermittent abdominal pain (child draws up knees)
currant jelly stool (blood and mucus mixed — late sign)
lethargy (child appears well between episodes then suddenly distressed)
visual_indicators: child crying and drawing legs to abdomen in spasms
immediate_actions: Air or contrast enema reduction (if <24 hours, no perforation)
Emergency surgery if enema fails or perforation suspected
content:
Intussusception is a surgical emergency where one segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent segment, causing bowel obstruction and ischemia. It is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children 3 months to 3 years. The classic triad is intermittent severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and red 'currant jelly' stool.
Symptoms: sudden severe intermittent abdominal pain (child draws up knees), vomiting (initially non-bilious), currant jelly stool (blood and mucus mixed — late sign), pallor, lethargy (child appears well between episodes then suddenly distressed)
Visual signs: child crying and drawing legs to abdomen in spasms, pale and sweating during pain, 'sausage-shaped' abdominal mass on palpation (right side), currant jelly (dark red mucusy) stool

description: Cerebral malaria is a severe neurological complication of Plasmodium falciparum malaria, caused by sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in cerebral microvessels. It presents with seizures, impaired consciousness, and coma in young children, carrying 15–20% mortality even with treatment. Immediate IV artesunate and supportive ICU care are required.
visual_indicators: abnormal eye movements or gaze deviation
Malarial retinopathy on fundoscopy (papilledema, vessel discoloration)
future_warnings: neurological sequelae (epilepsy, cognitive impairment, hemiplegia) in 10–24% of survivors
immediate_actions: Check and correct blood glucose urgently
content:
Cerebral malaria is a severe neurological complication of Plasmodium falciparum malaria, caused by sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in cerebral microvessels. It presents with seizures, impaired consciousness, and coma in young children, carrying 15–20% mortality even with treatment. Immediate IV artesunate and supportive ICU care are required.
Symptoms: impaired consciousness or coma, generalized seizures, high fever, abnormal posturing, irregular breathing, deep coma (Blantyre/Glasgow coma scale reduced)
Visual signs: unresponsive child with fever, seizures that don't stop, abnormal eye movements or gaze deviation, Malarial retinopathy on fundoscopy (papilledema, vessel discoloration)

description: Thalassemia is a group of inherited hemoglobin disorders resulting in reduced or absent alpha or beta globin chain synthesis, causing hemolytic anemia of varying severity. Thalassemia major (beta) requires regular blood transfusions and chelation therapy. It is most common in the Mediterranean, Middle East, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.
symptoms: skeletal deformities from marrow expansion (prominent forehead, cheekbones)
visual_indicators: 'chipmunk facies' or prominent skull bones in thalassemia major
future_warnings: transfusion-related iron overload → heart failure, cirrhosis, diabetes
immediate_actions: Chelation therapy (deferasirox or deferoxamine) for iron overload
content:
Thalassemia is a group of inherited hemoglobin disorders resulting in reduced or absent alpha or beta globin chain synthesis, causing hemolytic anemia of varying severity. Thalassemia major (beta) requires regular blood transfusions and chelation therapy. It is most common in the Mediterranean, Middle East, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.
Symptoms: pallor and fatigue, jaundice (yellow skin/eyes), dark urine, splenomegaly (enlarged spleen), skeletal deformities from marrow expansion (prominent forehead, cheekbones), growth retardation, gallstones
Visual signs: pallor (pale skin, conjunctiva, palms), jaundice, enlarged abdomen (spleen and liver), 'chipmunk facies' or prominent skull bones in thalassemia major

description: G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymatic disorder of red blood cells, affecting over 400 million people worldwide. It is X-linked and predominantly affects males. Triggers (oxidant drugs, infections, fava beans) can cause acute hemolytic anemia. Most individuals are asymptomatic between episodes.
symptoms: sudden onset pallor and jaundice during trigger exposure
abdominal or back pain during hemolytic episode
visual_indicators: rapid clinical deterioration with trigger exposure
future_warnings: acute hemolytic anemia with oxidant triggers (primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, fava beans)
immediate_actions: Avoid known oxidant drugs and foods (fava beans)
age_group: All ages (neonates at risk for jaundice)
content:
G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymatic disorder of red blood cells, affecting over 400 million people worldwide. It is X-linked and predominantly affects males. Triggers (oxidant drugs, infections, fava beans) can cause acute hemolytic anemia. Most individuals are asymptomatic between episodes.
Symptoms: sudden onset pallor and jaundice during trigger exposure, dark brown or red urine (hemoglobinuria), fatigue and weakness, rapid heart rate, abdominal or back pain during hemolytic episode, neonatal jaundice (severe form)
Visual signs: sudden pallor and jaundice, dark cola-colored urine, rapid clinical deterioration with trigger exposure

description: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited hemoglobin disorder where abnormal hemoglobin S causes red blood cells to deform into sickle shapes under low-oxygen conditions, causing vaso-occlusion, hemolytic anemia, and organ damage. Vaso-occlusive crises cause severe pain. Daily prophylactic penicillin and folic acid are standard in young children.
symptoms: painful vaso-occlusive crises (bones, joints, chest, abdomen)
dactylitis (swollen painful fingers in infants — often first presentation)
future_warnings: stroke (10% of children without transcranial doppler screening)
acute chest syndrome (pneumonia-like, can be fatal)
immediate_actions: Oral rehydration and fluids during crisis
Pain management (ibuprofen, stronger opioids for severe)
content:
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited hemoglobin disorder where abnormal hemoglobin S causes red blood cells to deform into sickle shapes under low-oxygen conditions, causing vaso-occlusion, hemolytic anemia, and organ damage. Vaso-occlusive crises cause severe pain. Daily prophylactic penicillin and folic acid are standard in young children.
Symptoms: painful vaso-occlusive crises (bones, joints, chest, abdomen), severe anemia and pallor, jaundice, dactylitis (swollen painful fingers in infants — often first presentation), splenomegaly in early childhood, frequent infections, stroke in children
Visual signs: pale conjunctiva and skin, jaundice, dactylitis (swollen red fingers/toes in infants), child in acute severe pain

description: Neonatal jaundice (neonatal hyperbilirubinemia) is yellowing of the skin and eyes in newborns due to elevated bilirubin, occurring in about 60% of term newborns. Most cases are physiological and self-limiting, but severe or rapid-onset jaundice can cause bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) and permanent brain damage if not treated promptly.
symptoms: yellow skin starting from face and moving downward
dark urine and pale stools (in obstructive causes)
irritability or high-pitched cry (danger sign — bilirubin encephalopathy)
visual_indicators: yellow skin in bright light (blanch skin to check)
checking Kramer's zones to assess extent (face, chest, abdomen, legs, palms/soles)
future_warnings: kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy → cerebral palsy, deafness, intellectual disability)
immediate_actions: Transcutaneous bilirubin measurement or serum bilirubin
Phototherapy (blue light) if above treatment threshold
Exchange transfusion for extremely high levels
Feed frequently to promote bilirubin excretion
Identify underlying cause (G6PD, ABO incompatibility, infection)
content:
Neonatal jaundice (neonatal hyperbilirubinemia) is yellowing of the skin and eyes in newborns due to elevated bilirubin, occurring in about 60% of term newborns. Most cases are physiological and self-limiting, but severe or rapid-onset jaundice can cause bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) and permanent brain damage if not treated promptly.
Symptoms: yellow skin starting from face and moving downward, yellow whites of eyes (scleral icterus), poor feeding or sleepiness, dark urine and pale stools (in obstructive causes), irritability or high-pitched cry (danger sign — bilirubin encephalopathy)
Visual signs: yellow skin in bright light (blanch skin to check), yellow sclera, checking Kramer's zones to assess extent (face, chest, abdomen, legs, palms/soles)

description: Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten (wheat, rye, barley) in genetically susceptible individuals, causing small intestinal villous atrophy and malabsorption. Presentation varies from classic diarrhea and failure to thrive in infants to subtle symptoms (iron deficiency, short stature) in older children. A strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the only treatment.
symptoms: poor weight gain or weight loss
iron deficiency anemia not responding to supplementation
future_warnings: failure to thrive and permanent growth impairment if undiagnosed
nutritional deficiencies (iron, vitamin D, calcium, B12)
increased risk of intestinal lymphoma (untreated adults)
immediate_actions: Anti-tTG IgA antibody test (and total IgA)
content:
Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten (wheat, rye, barley) in genetically susceptible individuals, causing small intestinal villous atrophy and malabsorption. Presentation varies from classic diarrhea and failure to thrive in infants to subtle symptoms (iron deficiency, short stature) in older children. A strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the only treatment.
Symptoms: chronic diarrhea (fatty, foul-smelling stools), abdominal bloating and distension, poor weight gain or weight loss, short stature and delayed puberty, iron deficiency anemia not responding to supplementation, fatigue, mouth ulcers
Visual signs: pot-belly (abdominal distension) with thin limbs, pale or grey fatty stools, generalized pallor from anemia

description: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections in children, caused primarily by Escherichia coli. Presentation varies by age — neonates may present with non-specific fever and poor feeding while older children have classic dysuria and frequency. Recurrent UTIs in young children warrant imaging to exclude vesicoureteral reflux.
symptoms: fever (may be the only sign in infants)
bedwetting in a previously dry child
vomiting and poor feeding in infants
visual_indicators: no localizing signs in infants despite fever
future_warnings: chronic kidney disease from renal scarring
immediate_actions: Clean catch urine culture before antibiotics
Oral trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin for lower UTI (school age)
IV ceftriaxone for febrile UTI in infants
Renal ultrasound for first febrile UTI under 2 years
content:
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections in children, caused primarily by Escherichia coli. Presentation varies by age — neonates may present with non-specific fever and poor feeding while older children have classic dysuria and frequency. Recurrent UTIs in young children warrant imaging to exclude vesicoureteral reflux.
Symptoms: fever (may be the only sign in infants), painful/burning urination (dysuria), frequent urination, cloudy or foul-smelling urine, abdominal or flank pain, bedwetting in a previously dry child, vomiting and poor feeding in infants
Visual signs: crying during urination, cloudy or discolored urine, no localizing signs in infants despite fever
